subject: Pathology
summary: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia (FNH) is a benign liver lesion with a characteristic central stellate scar. It has no malignant potential, no association with oral contraceptives, and rarely causes symptoms.

sections.p: FNH is a non‑neoplastic hyperplastic lesion of hepatocytes that forms a well‑circumscribed nodule, usually discovered incidentally on imaging.
b: Central stellate scar on imaging or histology is pathognomonic
Uniform hepatocyte plates with normal architecture
Absence of atypia or vascular invasion

t.b: Does the lesion show arterial hyperenhancement and a central scar that becomes iso‑ or hyperintense on delayed phase? → Typical FNH pattern; supports diagnosis.
Is the lesion iso‑ or slightly hyperechoic with a central scar and normal vascular flow? → Suggests FNH; helps rule out hemangioma.
Does histology show normal hepatocytes, bile duct proliferation, and a central scar? → Confirms FNH; avoid if classic imaging present.

sections.p: FNH is not staged; severity is judged by size, symptoms, and complications.
b: Lesions <5 cm are usually asymptomatic
Large (>5 cm) or symptomatic lesions may need intervention

sections.p: Exact cause unknown; thought to be a hyperplastic response to a vascular anomaly.
b: Congenital arterial malformation (most accepted hypothesis)
Hormonal influences (no proven link to OCPs)
Prior liver injury or inflammation

sections.p: Most patients are asymptomatic; when symptoms occur they relate to mass effect.
b: Incidental liver nodule on imaging
Right‑upper‑quadrant discomfort
Rarely, palpable abdominal mass

sections.p: Imaging is the cornerstone; labs are usually normal.
b: Liver function tests typically within reference range
Alpha‑fetoprotein normal, helps exclude hepatocellular carcinoma

t.b: Is AFP elevated? → Normal AFP supports benign lesion; elevation suggests malignancy.
Does the lesion show arterial phase hyperenhancement with a central scar? → Consistent with FNH; if unavailable, rely on MRI.

sections.p: FNH rarely causes serious problems, but vigilance for atypical features is essential.
b: Rapid growth >2 cm/yr
New onset pain or jaundice
Imaging features atypical for FNH (e.g., washout on portal phase)

sections.p: Observation is first‑line; intervene only for symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty.
b: Regular imaging follow‑up for lesions >5 cm or symptomatic
Surgical resection or laparoscopic ablation if pain, growth, or uncertainty persists

sections.p: No specific prevention; schedule periodic imaging based on lesion size and symptoms.
b: Ultrasound or MRI every 1–2 years for lesions >5 cm
No follow‑up needed for stable lesions <3 cm

sections.p: Other benign liver tumors share imaging characteristics.
b: Hepatic hemangioma – peripheral nodular enhancement, no central scar
Hepatocellular adenoma – association with OCPs, risk of hemorrhage
Focal hepatic metastasis – irregular borders, atypical enhancement
Central scar may be absent in small lesions, leading to misdiagnosis as adenoma
Arterial hyperenhancement alone can suggest HCC; need delayed phase to confirm scar

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain suggesting hemorrhage
Rapid increase in lesion size on imaging

faq.a: No, FNH has no malignant potential and does not progress to cancer.
Current evidence shows no causal link between OCP use and FNH.

faq.q: Can FNH rupture like a hemangioma?
faq.a: Rupture is exceedingly rare; FNH is considered non‑rupturing.

exam: Describe the imaging features that differentiate FNH from hepatic hemangioma.
Explain why biopsy is usually unnecessary in classic FNH.
List the red‑flag signs that would prompt surgical referral for a patient with FNH.
